title: Hubel and Wiesel: simple and complex cells
text:
CHAPTER 8. VISION
SECTION 8.2. HUBEL AND WIESEL: SIMPLE AND COMPLEX CELLS

Two young researchers and a slide projector

In 1958, David Hubel (1926 to 2013), a Canadian-born physician and neurophysiologist, and Torsten Wiesel (born 1924), a Swedish physician, began working together in Stephen Kuffler's laboratory at Johns Hopkins University. Kuffler had just characterized the center-surround receptive fields of retinal ganglion cells in the cat (section 8.1). The natural next question was: what happens in the visual cortex? Do cortical neurons also have center-surround receptive fields, or do they do something different?

Hubel had developed a tungsten microelectrode, sharpened electrolytically and insulated with lacquer, that could record the action potentials of single neurons in the cortex for long periods, even in awake animals. Hubel and Wiesel used it to record from neurons in the primary visual cortex of anesthetized cats, while projecting visual stimuli onto a screen in front of the cat's eyes.

At first, they used the same stimuli that had worked so well in the retina: small spots of light, projected with a modified ophthalmoscope and later a slide projector, using glass slides with spots painted on them. The cortical neurons responded poorly or not at all. After hours of frustration on one occasion, according to the story they told many times afterward, they finally got a strong response, not to a spot, but apparently to the edge of the glass slide itself as they inserted it into the projector. The slide's edge cast a faint shadow, a line, moving across the screen. The neuron fired vigorously when the line was at a particular orientation and much less at other orientations. This was the discovery of orientation selectivity.

The story is told in Hubel's and Wiesel's own accounts, including Hubel's Nobel lecture and their joint book Brain and Visual Perception (2005), so it comes from the people who were there, though any vivid story recalled years later may be simplified.

Hubel and Wiesel published their first paper on the cat visual cortex in 1959 in the Journal of Physiology, "Receptive fields of single neurones in the cat's striate cortex," followed by a major paper in 1962, "Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex." These papers are among the most cited in neuroscience.

Simple cells

Hubel and Wiesel found that many neurons in V1 had receptive fields that, like those of retinal ganglion cells, could be mapped with small spots into excitatory (ON) and inhibitory (OFF) regions. But the regions were not circular. They were elongated and arranged side by side: for example, a long narrow ON region flanked by two OFF regions, or an ON region next to an OFF region. Such a cell responds best to a line or edge of a particular orientation, at a particular position, matching its subregions. A bright bar on a dark background that falls on the ON region and avoids the OFF regions drives the cell strongly. Rotate the bar by 90 degrees, so it crosses all the subregions, and excitation and inhibition cancel.

Hubel and Wiesel called these "simple cells" because their responses could be predicted from the arrangement of ON and OFF subregions, roughly by summing the effects of light in each region. In other words, a simple cell behaves approximately like a linear filter with an oriented receptive field, followed by a threshold.

They proposed a beautifully simple model of how simple cells get their properties: a simple cell receives input from several LGN neurons whose center-surround receptive fields are arranged in a row in visual space. If the LGN cells are ON-center and their centers fall along a line, then the simple cell will be excited by a bright bar along that line. This "feedforward model" was a hypothesis, drawn in a famous diagram in their 1962 paper. Later experiments, particularly by R. Clay Reid and Jose-Manuel Alonso in the 1990s, who recorded simultaneously from connected LGN and cortical neurons, provided support for the idea that the LGN inputs to a simple cell are aligned with its subregions. Intracortical circuits also contribute to orientation selectivity, and the relative importance of feedforward and recurrent mechanisms was debated for a long time.

Mathematically, simple cell receptive fields are often well described by Gabor functions: a sinusoidal grating multiplied by a Gaussian envelope. In two dimensions:

  G(x, y) = exp( -(x'^2 + gamma^2 * y'^2) / (2*sigma^2) ) * cos( 2*pi*x'/lambda + phi )

where x' = x*cos(theta) + y*sin(theta) and y' = -x*sin(theta) + y*cos(theta) are coordinates rotated by the preferred orientation theta, lambda is the wavelength (inverse of spatial frequency), phi is the phase (determining whether the field looks like a bar or an edge), sigma is the size of the envelope, and gamma is its aspect ratio. The Gabor function was introduced in signal processing by the physicist Dennis Gabor in 1946, as an optimal compromise between localization in space (or time) and localization in frequency. In the 1980s, John Daugman and also Judson Jones and Larry Palmer showed that Gabor functions fit cat simple cell receptive fields well. Thus each simple cell is like a local spatial frequency analyzer tuned to an orientation, position, scale, and phase. Engineers will recognize this as a localized, oriented band-pass filter, related to wavelets.

Complex cells

Hubel and Wiesel found a second type of V1 neuron, which they called "complex cells." Complex cells are also orientation selective: they respond best to a line or edge of a particular orientation. But unlike simple cells, their receptive fields cannot be divided into separate ON and OFF regions. A complex cell responds to a properly oriented line anywhere within its receptive field, and it often responds to both bright and dark bars. Many complex cells respond best to a moving line, and some are direction selective, preferring motion in one direction over the opposite one.

So complex cells are tuned to orientation but are invariant (tolerant) to the exact position and polarity of the stimulus within their receptive field. Hubel and Wiesel proposed that a complex cell receives input from several simple cells, all with the same preferred orientation but with receptive fields at slightly different positions. If any of these simple cells is active, the complex cell fires. This is a kind of OR operation, or pooling.

A standard modern model of complex cells is the "energy model," proposed by Edward Adelson and James Bergen in 1985 for motion and applied to complex cells: the complex cell's response is the sum of the squared outputs of two simple-cell-like linear filters with the same orientation and spatial frequency but phases differing by 90 degrees (a quadrature pair, such as a cosine Gabor and a sine Gabor):

  response = (G_cos * I)^2 + (G_sin * I)^2

where G * I denotes the filter applied to the image I. This sum of squares is insensitive to the exact position of an edge within the receptive field (like the amplitude of a complex number, which does not depend on its phase), but remains sensitive to orientation and spatial frequency. It is the "local energy" of the image in a particular orientation and frequency band.

Hypercomplex cells and the hierarchy

Hubel and Wiesel also described cells that responded best to lines of a particular length, being inhibited when the line extended beyond the receptive field. They called these "hypercomplex" cells; today this property is called end-stopping, and it is considered a property of some simple and complex cells rather than a separate class. They extended their work to higher visual areas (V2 and V3, then called areas 18 and 19 in the cat), where they found cells with more elaborate properties.

From these results, Hubel and Wiesel proposed a hierarchical model of visual processing: center-surround cells in the retina and LGN feed into simple cells, which feed into complex cells, which feed into hypercomplex cells, and so on. At each stage, neurons respond to more complex features and are more tolerant of variations in position. This hierarchical view, with alternating stages of feature detection and pooling, is the conceptual ancestor of convolutional neural networks, as we will see in section 8.3. The strict hierarchy turned out to be too simple: many complex cells receive direct input from the LGN, and there are extensive recurrent and feedback connections. But the principle of building increasingly complex and invariant representations through successive stages has proved very influential.

Functional architecture: columns and maps

Hubel and Wiesel also discovered how these neurons are organized in the cortex. When they advanced the electrode perpendicular to the cortical surface, through the layers, all the neurons they encountered tended to have the same preferred orientation. When they advanced the electrode at an angle, roughly parallel to the surface, the preferred orientation shifted gradually and systematically, rotating through the full 180 degrees over a distance of roughly a millimeter, with occasional jumps. This led to the concept of orientation columns: vertical columns of neurons sharing an orientation preference, arranged across the cortex so that orientation changes smoothly.

The idea of cortical columns had been introduced by Vernon Mountcastle in 1957 for the somatosensory cortex, where he found columns of neurons responding to the same type of touch stimulus. Hubel and Wiesel found the same principle in vision.

They also found that many V1 neurons respond to stimuli in both eyes (binocular) but with a preference for one eye (ocular dominance). Neurons with the same eye preference are grouped into ocular dominance columns, which in the monkey form alternating stripes about half a millimeter wide for the left and right eyes. These stripes were visualized anatomically by injecting radioactive tracer into one eye, which was transported to the cortex, revealing the stripes in autoradiographs (work by Hubel, Wiesel, and Simon LeVay in the 1970s).

Putting these together, Hubel and Wiesel proposed the "ice cube" model of a "hypercolumn": a block of cortex about 1 millimeter square containing a full set of orientation columns for both eyes, processing one small region of the visual field. The visual cortex would be a repeated array of such modules, each analyzing its patch of the visual field for all orientations and both eyes.

Later, optical imaging of intrinsic signals, developed by Amiram Grinvald, Gary Blasdel, Tobias Bonhoeffer, and others in the 1980s and 1990s, revealed the actual layout of orientation maps across the surface of the cortex. The maps are not ice cubes; orientation preference changes smoothly in most places but is arranged around special points, called "pinwheel centers," where all orientations converge, like the spokes of a wheel. Interestingly, rodents such as mice and rats have orientation-selective neurons in V1 but do not have orientation columns; neurons with different preferences are intermixed in a "salt and pepper" arrangement. So columns are not necessary for orientation selectivity.

Development and critical periods

Hubel and Wiesel's other major contribution was the study of visual development. In the 1960s, they examined kittens in which one eye had been sutured closed during early life (monocular deprivation). They found that the deprived eye lost most of its ability to drive cortical neurons; the cortex became dominated by the open eye. This effect occurred only if deprivation took place during a "critical period" in early life (in cats, roughly the first few months); the same deprivation in adult cats had little effect. They showed that the anatomical ocular dominance stripes of the open eye expanded at the expense of those of the closed eye. These experiments had important medical implications: they helped explain amblyopia ("lazy eye") in children and the importance of treating congenital cataracts and strabismus early. We will return to critical periods in chapter 11.

Hubel and Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine "for their discoveries concerning information processing in the visual system." The other half of the prize went to Roger Sperry for his work on the functional specialization of the cerebral hemispheres (split-brain research).

Beyond V1: the visual hierarchy in primates

After V1, visual information flows through a series of cortical areas. Daniel Felleman and David Van Essen published in 1991 a famous diagram of the macaque visual system showing more than 30 visual areas connected by hundreds of pathways, organized into a hierarchy of levels based on the laminar patterns of their connections. Two major streams are commonly distinguished, following a proposal by Leslie Ungerleider and Mortimer Mishkin in 1982:

- The ventral stream, running from V1 through V2 and V4 to the inferior temporal cortex (IT), is involved in recognizing objects: the "what" pathway.
- The dorsal stream, running from V1 through V2 and the middle temporal area (MT, also called V5) to the posterior parietal cortex, is involved in processing motion and spatial location, and in guiding actions: the "where" or "how" pathway (the latter interpretation was proposed by Melvyn Goodale and David Milner in 1992).

Along the ventral stream, neurons become selective for increasingly complex features. In V4, neurons respond to curvature, contour shape, and color. In IT, some neurons respond selectively to complex objects, such as hands or faces, largely regardless of their position, size, and lighting. Charles Gross and colleagues reported neurons in monkey IT that responded to hands and faces in the early 1970s and 1980s, a finding initially met with skepticism. Later, using fMRI, Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues identified a region in the human fusiform gyrus that responds more strongly to faces than to other objects, the fusiform face area (described in 1997). Doris Tsao, Winrich Freiwald, Margaret Livingstone, and colleagues found clusters of face-selective cells ("face patches") in the macaque temporal lobe in the 2000s and showed that cells in these patches encode faces along specific dimensions of a face space. In 2017, Le Chang and Doris Tsao reported that face cells in macaque face patches encode faces as projections onto axes in a roughly 50-dimensional face space, allowing faces to be decoded and reconstructed from neural activity with good accuracy.

Bridge to AI: the blueprint for convolutional networks

Hubel and Wiesel's work gave AI three key ideas, all of which appear in convolutional neural networks.

Local receptive fields. Each simple cell looks at a small patch of the visual field. In a CNN, each unit in a convolutional layer receives input from a small patch (for example, 3 by 3 or 5 by 5 pixels) of the previous layer.

Feature detection with shared filters. Simple cells with the same orientation preference exist at every location. In a CNN, the same filter (feature detector) is applied at every location, producing a "feature map." This is weight sharing, which makes the network equivariant to translation (shifting the input shifts the feature map). Networks learn filters in their first layer that look like Gabor functions and center-surround filters, as if rediscovering V1 from data.

Pooling for invariance. Complex cells pool over simple cells at nearby positions, gaining tolerance to position. In a CNN, pooling layers (such as max pooling, which takes the maximum over a small neighborhood) do the same. Alternating convolution and pooling builds hierarchies of increasingly complex, increasingly invariant features, from edges to textures to parts to objects.

The column structure also has a loose analog: in a CNN, each location in a layer has a vector of feature responses, one for each filter, which is analogous to the full set of orientation columns in a hypercolumn processing one location.

Hubel and Wiesel's critical period experiments have a parallel too. Training a deep network with distorted or restricted data early in training can permanently impair performance, even if normal data are provided later. Alessandro Achille, Matteo Rovere, and Stefano Soatto reported "critical learning periods in deep networks" in 2019, explicitly inspired by Hubel and Wiesel, showing that a temporary deficit (such as blurred images) early in training caused lasting impairment in deep networks.

Summary

- Hubel and Wiesel, beginning in 1958, recorded single neurons in cat V1 and discovered orientation selectivity, reportedly after noticing a response to the edge of a slide.
- Simple cells have elongated ON and OFF subregions and act as oriented linear filters, often modeled as Gabor functions; Hubel and Wiesel proposed they are built from aligned LGN inputs.
- Complex cells are orientation selective but tolerant to position and polarity, modeled by pooling or by the energy model.
- They proposed a hierarchy of increasingly complex and invariant features, and discovered orientation and ocular dominance columns, organized in hypercolumns; optical imaging later revealed pinwheel maps.
- Monocular deprivation experiments revealed critical periods in development.
- They shared the 1981 Nobel Prize; later work mapped the ventral and dorsal streams and face-selective regions.
- Local receptive fields, shared filters, and pooling became the core of convolutional neural networks.
